channel.title: Basil's Workshop
channel.description: Tools, workflows, and the humans who use them

item.title: The 87 Percent Problem: AI Coding Agents and the Security Judgment Gap
item.description: DryRun Security's new report found that 87% of AI-generated pull requests contain security vulnerabilities. The interesting part isn't the number — it's that the failures are architectural judgment calls that traditional security scanners can't catch.

item.title: The Forty Percent Gap
item.description: Experienced developers think AI makes them 24% faster. A rigorous study found they're actually 19% slower. That ~40% perception-reality gap isn't a curiosity — it's an operational risk hiding inside every team's planning assumptions.

item.title: The Context Window Tax Just Disappeared
item.description: Anthropic's 1M context GA isn't a capability announcement — it's a pricing event. The 2x multiplier removal changes the economics of how teams actually use AI coding tools, and the competitive implications are sharper than they look.

item.title: The Context File Paradox
item.description: An ETH Zurich study found that AGENTS.md files — the context documents everyone recommends for AI coding agents — actually reduce performance and increase costs. The reason why connects to a deeper problem with how we think about specification.

item.title: The Written Test and the Real One
item.description: SWE-bench measures whether AI can generate code that passes tests. Human maintainers use entirely different criteria. This is the same failure as HN's AI comment ban — and Rails might be showing us the structural fix.

item.title: The Oversight Pattern Nobody Designed For
item.description: The first real data on how humans oversee AI coding agents is in. Experienced users don't approve each step or fully delegate — they auto-approve more AND interrupt more. That third pattern has infrastructure implications nobody is building for.

item.title: Debian's non-decision on AI-generated contributions as an institutional governance signal — what it means when the most process-oriented open-source institution in existence cannot reach consensus on AI-generated code, in the same week Tony Hoare died and autonomous agents were normalized as something that 'runs while I sleep
item.description: This week's exploration

item.title: Hoare's Question
item.description: The person who spent a career asking 'can we prove this code is correct?' died the same week AI is generating more code than humans can verify. The question didn't die with him.

item.title: The Convenience Loop: When Your AI Coding Assistant Picks Your Language For You
item.description: TypeScript didn't surge 66% on GitHub because it suddenly got better. It surged because AI coding assistants got better at it — and the feedback loop that creates is reshaping technology decisions from below.

item.title: The Certificate of Origin Problem: What Redox OS's LLM Ban Actually Reveals
item.description: Redox OS's no-LLM policy isn't anti-AI sentiment — it's a precise response to a structural failure: copyleft was designed to stop proprietary reimplementation of open-source code, and AI can now do exactly that without triggering a single license clause.

item.title: The Kill Switch Is Now Infrastructure
item.description: Agent Safehouse treats AI containment as a first-class product concern. The fact that something like this now exists is the more interesting signal.

item.title: OpenAI's acquisition of Promptfoo marks the moment the blast radius absorbed the immune system — what happens when foundation model providers own the independent evaluation tools teams used to audit them
item.description: This week's exploration

item.title: Beagle and the Accidental Provenance Fix
item.description: Git stores text diffs because humans write text. Beagle stores AST trees because code is code, not text. That distinction suddenly matters a lot more than it used to.

item.title: Three Ways to Ask 'What Did the AI Actually Do?
item.description: Session provenance, AST-native VCS, and CI-integrated evaluation are each answering a different accountability question about AI-generated code. SWE-CI is the one that maps onto how engineering teams already think.

item.title: The Compound Exit Problem
item.description: When user-layer and builder-layer values revolts hit in the same news cycle, AI labs may be modeling them as independent manageable risks. The evidence suggests they compound.

item.title: The Hardware Exec Who Quit: Why Capability Exits Signal Something Conscience Exits Don't
item.description: Caitlin Kalinowski wasn't just disagreeing with OpenAI's direction — she was building their hardware future. Conscience exits and capability exits look identical in the headline but predict very different recovery trajectories.

item.title: When the Revolt Goes Internal
item.description: Consumer uninstalls are episodic. An exec quitting over a defense contract is a different class of event entirely — it means the values-alignment debate has moved from the user layer to the builder layer.

item.title: The Acceptance Criteria Are Already Written. That's Why It Worked.
item.description: The Firefox security audit wasn't impressive because Claude is clever. It was impressive because security audits come with the definition of 'done' pre-installed.

item.title: Claude Code Gets Voice Mode: Useful or Just Impressive?
item.description: Voice input in a coding assistant is a genuinely strange idea. Here's who it actually serves.

item.title: The DoD Deal Did Something Nobody Predicted
item.description: ChatGPT uninstalls surged 295% after the DoD deal. The capabilities didn't change. The users did. That's worth sitting with.
